The Hooded merganser (Lophodytes cucullatus) is a cavity-nesting waterfowl species whose hatchlings emerge at a relatively advanced stage of development, a trait typical of precocial birds. Freshly laid eggs have an initial wet weight of approximately 59 grams [Ww0 = approximately 59 grams], and when incubated at a stable temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] require a developmental period of 33 days [ab = 33 days] before the downy chicks break through the shell. Upon hatching, these neonates exhibit a modest body mass of approximately 35.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 35.4 grams], a value that reflects their substantial yolk reserves at the point of emergence. This initial weight is considerably less than the species' recorded extremes for adult body size, highlighting the dramatic growth trajectory that must be accomplished during the early post-hatching phase. The nestlings, although capable of leaving the nest cavity within a day or two, remain dependent on parental provisioning for several weeks as they develop their flight feathers and foraging skills.

Under the thermal regime typical of the species' active metabolic period, which corresponds to a body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], the developmental timeline from hatching to nutritional independence is tightly constrained. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 70 days after hatching [tx = 70 days after hatching], a duration that aligns with the extended parental care period observed in other cavity-nesting ducks at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. Following fledging, the young birds enter a protracted juvenile phase during which they refine their diving and prey-capture abilities. The attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, is delayed substantially relative to fledging, occurring at 210 days after hatching [tp = 210 days after hatching] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This relatively late onset of reproductive capability likely reflects the time required to acquire the somatic reserves and foraging proficiency necessary for successful breeding.

The reproductive output of the Hooded merganser, measured under field conditions at a body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], follows a pattern typical of many cavity-nesting anatids. Females lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with clutch sizes ranging from 7 to 15 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 7 to 15 eggs per clutch], as documented in the Animal Diversity Web. This translates to an annual reproductive effort that is modest compared to some dabbling ducks, which may renest multiple times following clutch loss. The energy invested in each egg is considerable, and the female's body condition at the time of laying is a strong predictor of clutch size. Brood parasitism, both intra- and interspecific, has been reported but appears to occur at relatively low frequencies in most studied populations.

Considerable sexual dimorphism exists in the ultimate body size of adult Hooded mergansers, a pattern consistent with the species' courtship and mating system. Adult females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 768 grams [Wwi = 768 grams], whereas adult males reach a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 897 grams [Wwi = 897 grams]. This difference of over 120 grams between the sexes is largely attributable to the males' more robust skeletal structure and greater pectoral muscle mass, which confer advantages in aerial maneuverability and intrasexual competition. The species' resting metabolic rate, measured via respirometry at a body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], was recorded at 351.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 351.5 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic rate is intermediate among waterfowl of comparable body size, reflecting the species' active, pursuit-diving foraging strategy.

Longevity records for the Hooded merganser, compiled from banding returns and captive studies, indicate a maximum lifespan of 16.2 years [am = 16.2 years] under the standard metabolic temperature regime of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan for a duck of its size is consistent with the species' relatively slow life-history pace, characterized by delayed maturity and a single annual reproductive event. The timing of the first successful breeding attempt, or age at first brood, is typically observed at 2 years since birth [tR = 2 years since birth] when maintained at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This delay between reaching sexual maturity and actually producing a viable clutch highlights the importance of nest site acquisition and pair bond formation in this species, as suitable cavities are often a limiting resource in forested wetland habitats.
